aiPrompt.categorizationDescription: Categorize the document based on its content and the general proportional reasoning curriculum found in middle grades mathematics.

aiUnitSummary.overview: Shapes and Designs is a grade 7 geometry unit about what makes a shape the shape it is, framed by why builders brace with triangles and why bees build in hexagons. Investigation 1 works from side lengths: students build polygons from polystrips and find that a polygon closes only when the longest side is shorter than the sum of the others, that three lengths fix exactly one triangle while four lengths allow many quadrilaterals, and that triangles alone are rigid — so diagonals that decompose a polygon into triangles are what stiffen it. Investigation 2 turns to angles: benchmark angles and estimation on circular grids, measuring with a protractor or angle ruler, and the relationships among vertical, adjacent, supplementary and complementary angles where lines cross. Investigation 3 joins the two, deriving the interior angle sum S = 180(n − 2), the constant 360° exterior sum, which regular polygons tile a plane and why, and finally which combinations of sides and angles determine a unique shape.

entries.priorKnowledge: From grade 6: naming and classifying polygons by number of sides; measuring lengths; recognising triangles and quadrilaterals. From Data About Us: recording results in a table, looking for patterns in collected data, and describing them. No prior work on angle measure or on the conditions for a shape to exist is assumed.
entries.problemDigest: Opens the unit by asking which sets of three lengths can actually make a triangle. Students pick three numbers between 2 and 20, build with polystrips or the digital equivalent, try to make a second different triangle from the same three lengths, and tabulate what worked. Two results come out of the data: a triangle exists only when the sum of the two shorter sides exceeds the longest, and when it exists it is unique — unlike later shapes, three lengths leave no freedom. The What If section applies this to Geraldo's tent, where four 3-foot, two 5-foot, one 6-foot and one 7-foot poles are available and students enumerate every triangular doorframe possible, then choose one and justify it; 3-3-6 and 3-3-7 are the instructive failures.
entries.approachGuidance: Students generate their own side lengths and collect results before any rule is stated. Let the pattern come from their data rather than supplying the triangle inequality.

entries.priorKnowledge: That three lengths make a triangle only when the two shorter sides sum to more than the longest, and that such a triangle is unique; building and recording shapes from given side lengths; reading a pattern out of a table of results.
entries.problemDigest: Repeats the side-length experiment for quadrilaterals and then generalises. Students build from four lengths between 2 and 20, try to make a second different quadrilateral from the same four, and record what happens. The contrast with 1.1 is the point: four lengths that close at all close in many ways, and the order of the sides matters — 3, 4, 3, 4 gives a parallelogram while 3, 3, 4, 4 gives a kite. The What If section follows Michal into pentagons and hexagons and arrives at the general condition, that the longest side must be shorter than the sum of all the others, or the remaining sides flatten out with no angle left to close the shape. Students also build the largest polygon their set of strips allows.
entries.approachGuidance: Students choose their own lengths and extend the question to polygons of their own choosing. Support the generalisation they are building rather than stating it for them.

entries.priorKnowledge: The side-length condition for a polygon to close; that three lengths determine a unique triangle while four or more do not; that a diagonal joins two non-adjacent vertices; building polygons from strips and tabulating results.
entries.problemDigest: Asks why triangles are used as braces, by testing rigidity directly. Students predict the minimum number of diagonals needed to make an n-sided polygon rigid, then build triangles, quadrilaterals, pentagons and hexagons and find the least number of diagonals that stops each flexing, repeating with differently shaped examples of the same polygon. The What If section gives Beatrice's observation that the minimum set of diagonals decomposes the shape into triangles, and asks students to say why that explains the rigidity. This closes Investigation 1 by connecting the earlier result — that three sides fix one triangle — to the structural fact that only triangles hold their shape.
entries.approachGuidance: Students predict first, then test with their own shapes. Work from what their building actually showed rather than confirming the expected number of diagonals.

entries.priorKnowledge: Side-length conditions for polygons and the rigidity of triangles from Investigation 1; reading coordinates; the idea of a full turn. From Data About Us: collecting data, representing it and looking for patterns. Angle measure in degrees is introduced here rather than assumed.
entries.problemDigest: Introduces angle as an amount of turn and builds a set of benchmarks. Students play Four in a Row on circular grids marked at 30° and 45°, naming points by their coordinates on the grid and developing winning strategies — the game is the vehicle for reading angles off a polar grid. They then mark the benchmark angles 30°, 45°, 60°, 90°, 120°, 180° and 270° and use them to estimate unmeasured angles. The What If section works through Amit's benchmark estimates for four angles, including one estimated as a full turn minus a known angle, and then has students judge other students' estimation claims. The closing discussion collects the benchmarks as fractions of a turn.
entries.approachGuidance: Estimation strategies and game strategies both vary between students, and several are compared. Support a student's own benchmark reasoning rather than a single method.

entries.priorKnowledge: Angle as an amount of turn, measured in degrees; the benchmark angles 30°, 45°, 60°, 90°, 120°, 180°, 270° and 360° and their use in estimating; reading angles on a circular grid; that estimates should be checked against a measurement.
entries.problemDigest: Moves from estimating angles to measuring them with an angle ruler or protractor, in two contexts. In the honeybee waggle dance, decoded by Karl von Frisch, the angle between the bee's run and straight up — which represents the sun — gives the direction to the flowers, and the length of the run is proportional to the distance; students estimate then measure the angles for several days, and sketch given angles of 180° and 120°. The What If section turns to Amelia Earhart's 1937 flight, estimating and then measuring how many degrees off course the Nikumaroro crash site lies from Howland Island, and asking where a plane 20° south of the intended course from New Guinea would arrive. The closing question weighs estimation against measurement.
entries.approachGuidance: Both contexts ask students to estimate first and then measure, and to weigh the two. Treat the estimate as worth reasoning about rather than a step to be replaced by the measurement.

entries.priorKnowledge: Measuring and estimating angles with benchmarks, an angle ruler or a protractor; angle as an amount of turn; that a straight line is 180° and a full turn 360°; parallel lines as lines that stay the same distance apart.
entries.problemDigest: Names the angle relationships formed when lines cross. Vertical angles sit opposite each other at a vertex; adjacent angles share a side and vertex without overlapping; two angles are supplementary when they sum to 180° and complementary when they sum to 90°. The challenge gives three parallel lines cut by a transversal and asks what students notice, what they can measure, and which pairs are vertical, supplementary, adjacent or complementary. The What If section tests whether those relationships survive in two further figures — one with parallel lines, one without — which is where corresponding angles are seen to be equal only in the parallel case. The closing discussion is that these relationships let you find missing angles without measuring every one.
entries.approachGuidance: Students notice and conjecture relationships before testing them on new figures. Support the conjecture a student is testing rather than naming the relationships first.

entries.priorKnowledge: Angle measure, benchmark angles and measuring tools; vertical, adjacent, supplementary and complementary angles; that a full turn is 360°; polygon names and the side-length conditions from Investigation 1.
entries.problemDigest: Asks why bees build in hexagons, by working out which shapes tile a plane. Students predict which of a given shape set will cover a surface without gaps or overlaps, then test each shape by duplicating and fitting copies, recording for each whether it tiles and what the angles total where the shapes meet — always 360° where a tiling succeeds. The What If section gives Maisie's argument: a regular hexagon's vertex angle is 120°, so three meet exactly at a point, and no regular polygon with more than six sides can tile because its vertex angles exceed 120° and two are already too few to reach 360°. The closing discussion notes that bees could have used triangles or quadrilaterals, and that hexagons give the most storage area.
entries.approachGuidance: Students test shapes themselves and build the 360° criterion from what they find. Let the rule emerge from their tiling attempts rather than stating it in advance.

entries.priorKnowledge: Which polygons tile and that the angles meeting at a point in a tiling total 360°; vertical, supplementary and complementary angles; measuring and estimating angles; that a regular polygon has equal angles.
entries.problemDigest: Derives the interior angle sum of any polygon. Devon tears the corners off a triangle and rearranges them into a straight line, showing the sum is 180°; students test whether the argument holds for other triangles and other polygons by tearing and rearranging shapes from the set and tabulating the results, finding that each extra side adds 180° and so that S = 180(n − 2). The What If section compares three further derivations: Trevor draws diagonals from one vertex, cutting an n-gon into n − 2 triangles; Casey draws segments from an interior point instead; and Maria uses parallel lines to establish the triangle sum itself. The closing discussion extends this to the measure of a single angle in a regular polygon.
entries.approachGuidance: Four different derivations of the same formula are set side by side. Help students see why each works rather than promoting one as the proper proof.

entries.priorKnowledge: The interior angle sum S = 180(n − 2) and the angle of a regular polygon; supplementary angles; that a full turn is 360°; measuring angles; decomposing polygons into triangles.
entries.problemDigest: Introduces exterior angles, formed by extending a side, and establishes that they sum to 360° for any polygon. Cyclists ride a pentagonal training circuit, turning through an exterior angle at each vertex, and students work out the total turn for one lap without measuring — the argument being that a full lap returns you to your starting direction, so the turns total one complete rotation — then check by measuring. They repeat for triangles, quadrilaterals and hexagons of their own drawing. The What If section compares three students' generalisations: Amy's, which works but must be recalculated per shape; Neveah's, which uses variables and so covers any polygon; and Nic's, which is Neveah's idea stated only for a triangle. Students judge which generalise.
entries.approachGuidance: Students reason to the 360° result before measuring, and compare three students' generalisations. Value the argument and its generality over the arithmetic.

entries.priorKnowledge: The side-length conditions for polygons; that three side lengths fix a unique triangle; interior and exterior angle sums; vertical, supplementary and complementary angles; measuring and constructing angles and lengths; that a regular polygon's angles are equal.
entries.problemDigest: Pulls the unit together by asking what information determines a shape. A triangle is given with all its angles and sides, and students decide which of several short text messages carry enough information for someone else to reproduce it exactly — distinguishing messages that fix a unique triangle from those that fix only its shape, allowing any size, or that leave a side free to swing. The What If section works through a series of design briefs, deciding for each whether a polygon can be built at all, sketching it when it can, and saying whether it is unique; these include a set of lengths violating the triangle inequality, and angle sets given as x, 2x, 3x and x, 3x, 3x where students solve for the angles and find one is right-angled and the other isosceles.
entries.approachGuidance: Each design asks whether a shape is possible and whether it is unique, with several answers defensible until justified. Support the reasoning about sufficiency rather than producing a drawing.

entries.priorKnowledge: The whole unit: side-length conditions for polygons and the uniqueness of a triangle from three sides; the rigidity of triangles and the use of diagonals; angle as turn, benchmark angles, estimating and measuring; vertical, adjacent, supplementary and complementary angles, and corresponding angles across parallel lines; S = 180(n − 2), the 360° exterior sum, and the tiling criterion.
entries.problemDigest: The unit's three Mathematical Reflections, one per investigation, each asking what students now know about geometric shapes. The expected ground is the side-length condition and what it implies about uniqueness; why triangles are rigid and other polygons are not; reading, sketching and estimating angles with benchmarks and the limits of measurement; the named angle relationships at intersecting and parallel lines and their use in writing equations for missing angles; the interior angle sum and its formula; the constant exterior sum; and the 360° condition for tiling. A writing and discussion task with no new content.

entries.priorKnowledge: Whatever has been covered when the exercises are assigned; the banks are organised by investigation and are normally used alongside the corresponding problems rather than after the whole unit.
entries.problemDigest: The unit's ACE question banks — Applications, Connections and Extensions — gathered as one item and grouped by investigation rather than taught as a problem. Investigation 1's bank gives sets of three lengths and asks whether each builds a triangle, whether it is unique, and why some fail, introducing the isosceles, equilateral, scalene and right classifications through the examples. Investigation 2's bank covers classifying angles as acute, obtuse or right, reading snowboarders' 180, 540 and 720 as fractions of a turn, writing equations for a missing angle using supplementary and complementary relationships, and estimating against benchmarks. Investigation 3's bank is largely tiling and angle-sum work, including multiple-choice items on which regular polygons and combinations tile.
entries.approachGuidance: Many items ask for an explanation or a justification rather than only an answer. Support the reasoning the student offers rather than supplying the result.

investigations.title: SAD Investigation 1: Designing Polygons: The Side Connection

text:
Problem 1.1 Designing Triangles: The Side Connections

This Problem develops student understanding of the basic facts that in a triangle the sum of any two sides must be greater than the third; and that once three acceptable side lengths have been chosen, there is only one triangular shape with those side lengths. In the Initial Challenge students use Polystrips to find side lengths that will make triangles. The What If Situations will have them examine some specific triangles.

NWDYK

What combinations of three side lengths can be used to make a triangle? How many different triangles are possible for each combination?

Arc of Learning

Generalizing and Using Properties of Polygons: Introduction/Exploration

Algebraic Expressions and Equations: Introduction

Key Terms

Polygons

Regular Polygons

Materials

Learning Aid 1: Paper Polystrips (optional)

Learning Aid 1.1: Building Triangles

Polystrips and fasteners or digital polystrips

Virtual polystrips (alternate): https://media.pk12ls.com/curriculum/math/cmp3/activities/A82391/index.html

Pacing

1 Day

Groups

2-3

A #1-6

C #15-16

E #21

Facilitating Discourse

LAUNCH

Teacher Moves: Language

CONNECTING TO PRIOR KNOWLEDGE

As you are going over the Looking Ahead spend time discussing polygons and regular polygons. You might find it useful to initiate work on the Investigation by asking students where they have seen triangles used in structures and then why they think those extra braces are used.

Suggested question

  • What is it that makes triangles so common in construction?

Teacher Moves: Fist to Five, Make a Prediction

PRESENTING THE CHALLENGE

It is a good idea to demonstrate how to use the polystrips and how to make a triangle given the lengths. First, choose three numbers under 20, such as 6, 8, 12. Build a triangle with the polystrips using those numbers as side lengths. Then have each group build a 6-8-12 triangle. Check to see that each group knows how to fasten the strips together to represent the lengths.

Once they are comfortable with how to use the polystrips, have students work in groups of 2 -3 to complete this problem for other triangles to choose the lengths of sides for their possible triangles you could have students roll a number cube.

Suggested question

  • Will any three side lengths make a triangle?

EXPLORE

Teacher Moves: Restating

PROVIDING FOR INDIVIDUAL NEEDS

Make sure students produce sample sets of side lengths that can be used for constructing a triangle and other sample sets that cannot be used. Have students record the sets of side lengths that can be used to make a triangle versus those that cannot, so that they may draw their own conclusions from the data collected. As students continue to explore types of triangles using polystrips, encourage them to try to find patterns in the side lengths of the triangles they find. Asking students to restate how another person describes their conjecture can help a group to decide how to write it symbolically. For What If Situation A, some students may need some reminders of the definitions of equilateral, isosceles and right triangles

Teacher Moves: Selecting and Sequencing

PLANNING FOR THE SUMMARY

As you are circulating take note of the conjectures students have on the combinations of three side lengths that can be used to make a triangle. Encourage students to look for patterns in the data they have collected. Choose several examples from students that will make triangles and examples that will not to use in the summary.

SUMMARIZE

Teacher Moves: Claim, Support, Question

SOLUTIONS AND STRATEGIES

The most important result from this Problem is to answer the question, “What combinations of side lengths can and cannot be used to make a triangle?” Students should be able to articulate, in reasonably clear language, the principle that the sum of any two side lengths must always be greater than the third side length. They should be able to give an argument about why that is true, accompanied by a demonstration with polystrips.

MAKING THE MATHEMATICS EXPLICIT

Suggested questions

  • Can we come up with a summary statement that would help someone who is not here today know how to judge whether three lengths will make a triangle without actually building the triangle?
  • Which sets of side lengths form a triangle? Why?
  • Do any of these triangles have special properties? Describe them.
  • For What if Situation A, how could Giraldo make his triangular doorframe?
  • Do you have any What If questions?

As you finish the mathematical discussions, have students reflect on the Now What Do You Know question(s).

Problem 1.2 Designing Quadrilaterals: The Side Connection

The objective of this Problem is to extend the Triangle Inequality Property into a somewhat parallel result for quadrilaterals. The Initial Challenge will have students building quadrilaterals with different side lengths. The What If Situations will look at conjectures, reveal the fact that quadrilaterals are not rigid figures and investigate other polygons.

NWDYK

Describe what you learned from experiments in building triangles and quadrilaterals. How are different polygons similar and different? How do the differences explain the frequent use of triangles when building structures?

Arc of Learning

Generalizing and Using Properties of Polygons: Exploration

Algebraic Expressions and Equations: Introduction/Exploration
Key Terms

Materials

Learning Aid 1: Paper Polystrips (optional)

Learning Aid 1.2: Building Quadrilaterals

Polystrips and fasteners or digital polystrips

Pacing

1 Day

Groups

2-3

A #7-12

C #17-18

E #22

Facilitating Discourse

LAUNCH

CONNECTING TO PRIOR KNOWLEDGE

Discuss that the results of the sum of two side lengths is greater than the third side length for triangles and the uniqueness of the Side-Side-Side condition for triangles that students found in Problem 1.1.

Teacher Moves: Make Predictions

PRESENTING THE CHALLENGE

Suggested question

  • Can you make a quadrilateral using any four lengths for the sides? If so, is the shape unique?

Tell students they are going to conduct an experiment to gather data to help answer this question. They will look for relationships that will let them predict whether four line segments will make a quadrilateral without building it.

Explain to students that keeping an accurate record of their data is very important because it allows them to recreate examples as evidence of what they discovered.

EXPLORE

PROVIDING FOR INDIVIDUAL NEEDS

As students work on the Initial Challenge, make sure students keep the question, “Can you make a quadrilateral using any four lengths for the sides?” in mind. Encourage them to consider different arrangements of side lengths and to record differences in the shapes that may occur. Also, encourage students to make sketches of their quadrilaterals.

For What If Situation A, you may want to have half the room investigate pentagons and half the room investigate hexagons. Some groups may want to investigate other polygons as well.

PLANNING FOR THE SUMMARY

As students are working on making quadrilaterals look for examples that will make a quadrilateral and ones that do not. Use these examples in the Summary. Listen for the way students are talking about the side lengths necessary to create a quadrilateral.

SUMMARIZE

Teacher Moves: Gallery Walk

SOLUTIONS AND STRATEGIES

Each part of this Problem focuses on an important property of polygons, so it will be important to review student answers. You can start with a Gallery Walk for the Initial Challenge. Students should be able to justify answers to the questions:

  • Can any four lengths form a quadrilateral?
  • What is unique about the four side lengths that can be used build squares? Rectangles? Parallelograms?

Teacher Moves: Language

MAKING THE MATHEMATICS EXPLICIT

A summary of strategies for finding different quadrilaterals from a given set of side lengths should come from the discussion. Two powerful strategies that focus on different aspects of what determines a quadrilateral are the following:

  • Put the set of lengths together in different orders. (This technique highlights the role of side lengths in determining a shape.)
  • Build a quadrilateral from polystrips. Alter its shape by pressing on the sides or vertices of the quadrilateral. A quadrilateral with any give side lengths can form an infinite number of different quadrilaterals. (This technique highlights the role of angles in determining a shape and the lack of rigidity for quadrilaterals.)

If four side lengths make a quadrilateral, the shape is not unique. Ask for examples of this and put them on the board or poster paper. As the discussion continues, add other examples with descriptions.

Ask students to explain and record in their notes a clear answer to the build-and-stress activity questions. Ask whether a quadrilateral is rigid.

Finally, students should compare the relationships among side lengths of triangles with those of quadrilaterals. You may want to make a poster to show these findings. Include information about angle sums as well.

As you finish the mathematical discussions, have students reflect on the Now What Do You Know question(s).

Problem 1.3 Experimenting with Rigidity

In this Problem students will investigate shapes that aren’t very rigid and how to increase the rigidity with diagonals. Students will conduct an experiment in the Initial Challenge to find that the number of diagonals needed to make a polygon rigid is three less than the number of sides. Students will generalize in words and symbols the relationship between the number of diagonals creating embedded triangles in the polygons which make it rigid.

NWDYK

What do you know about the rigidity of shapes and how does this explain the frequent use of triangles in building structures?

Arc of Learning

Generalizing and Using Properties of Polygons: Introduction/Exploration

Algebraic Expressions and Equations: Introduction/Exploration
Key Terms

Materials

Learning Aid 1.3: Diagonals and Rigidity

Learning Aid 1.3B: Shapes (optional)

Pacing

1 Day

Groups

2

A #13-14

C #19-20

E #23

Facilitating Discourse

LAUNCH

CONNECTING TO PRIOR KNOWLEDGE

Revisit What If Situation B from Problem 1.2 on Beatrice’s Experiment with rigidity of triangles and quadrilaterals.

Teacher Moves: Making Predictions

PRESENTING THE CHALLENGE

Discuss the introduction of Beatrice’s wondering about adding diagonals to make polygons more rigid.

Suggested questions

  • What does it mean to be rigid?
  • Are triangles rigid? Quadrilaterals?
  • What do you think would happen if you added a diagonal to one of the quadrilaterals you made yesterday?

Explain the experiment in the Initial Challenge.

  • If a polygon with n sides is not rigid, what is the minimum number of diagonals needed to make it rigid?

EXPLORE

PROVIDING FOR INDIVIDUAL NEEDS

Circulate to see that students are building the polygons with diagonals correctly.

Suggested questions

  • How do you know that you have built a _________ (insert name of polygon)?
  • What tells you the shape is rigid?
  • Do you see a pattern in the data in your table?
  • Does your sketch give you any ideas on how many diagonals are needed?

Teacher Moves: Selecting and Sequencing

PLANNING FOR THE SUMMARY

As you are circulating during the Explore select student work to use in the Summary that will push the conversation on minimum number of diagonals needed to make a polygon rigid. Select polygons that students have made of various side lengths to use as examples. Listen for students who are finding the embedded triangles in the polygons as they add the diagonals.

SUMMARIZE

Teacher Moves: Compare Thinking

SOLUTIONS AND STRATEGIES

Have students share their polygons with diagonals that they made with polystrips. Have students share the conclusion they found for the minimum number of diagonals needed of an n-gon to make it rigid.

MAKING THE MATHEMATICS EXPLICIT

Suggested questions

  • Do you agree with _________’s polygon and the number of diagonals they have chosen?
  • What did you notice in your sketches of the polygons and the minimum number of diagonals?
  • What is the minimum number of diagonals for an n-gon?
  • Did this generalization work for a heptagon, octagon and/or nonagon?
  • Do you agree with Beatrice?
  • Does Beatrice’s observation about creating embedded triagonal when adding the diagonals appear in the polygons you made with the polystrips?

As you finish the mathematical discussions, have students reflect on the Now What Do You Know question(s).

Problem 2.1 In a Spin: Angles and Rotations

The goals of this Problem are to develop student understanding of angles as rotations or turns, as a geometric shape, and their awareness of common benchmark angles, the multiples of 30° and 45°. In the Initial Challenge students will play a game called Four In A Row where the object is to get four in a row on a circular grid with 30° or 45° intervals. In the What If Situations students will use this understanding to estimate given angles and draw angles.

NWDYK

How are benchmark angles useful in solving problems?

Arc of Learning

Generalizing and Using Properties of Polygons: Exploration/Analysis

Algebraic Expressions and Equations: Exploration

Key Terms

Angle

Degree

Right angle

Angle measures

Learning Aid 2.1A: Four in a Row

problems.title: SAD 2.2 The Bee Dance and Amelia Earhart
problems.subtitle: Measuring Angles and Distance

text:
Problem 2.2 The Bee Dance and Amelia Earhart: Measuring Angles and Distances

The goal of this Problem is to develop student understanding of two standard tools for angle measurement—the goniometer or angle ruler and the protractor. The contexts of the bee dance in the Initial Challenge and Amelia Earhart’s fateful journey in the What If Situations give a context for the purpose of accuracy in angle measurement.

NWDYK

What are the advantages and disadvantages of estimating angle measures? What are the advantages and disadvantages of using a protractor or angle ruler to measure an angle?

Arc of Learning

Generalizing and Using Properties of Polygons: Exploration/Analysis
Key Terms

Materials

Learning Aid 2.2A: Bees and Angle Measurements

Learning Aid 2.2B: Amelia Earhart

Teaching Aid 2.2: Using an Angle Ruler

Teacher Connection Videos (optional):

  • https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-7ijI-g4jHg
  • https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=bFDGPgXtK-U

Pacing

1-2 Days

Groups

2

A #7-12

C #23-25

E #30-31

Facilitating Discourse

LAUNCH

CONNECTING TO PRIOR KNOWLEDGE

Draw an angle and ask students to estimate its measure. Before students use a tool to measure an angle, they should have a reasonable estimate of the angle’s size so that they can tell if they have measured incorrectly. Tell students that in this Problem, they will use tools to measure the size of angles.

PRESENTING THE CHALLENGE

Introduce the tools, angle ruler and protractor. Demonstrate measuring an angle using each tool. The angle ruler reinforces angles as rotations, encourage students to use it as they are learning about angle measures being the opening between the two rays. Students are probably more familiar with protractors; however, to make sure students are using them correctly, you will need to review how to use them.

EXPLORE

Teacher Moves: Problem Solving Environment

PROVIDING FOR INDIVIDUAL NEEDS

As students use an angle ruler, monitor their work to be sure that they are placing the angle ruler correctly and reading the measures accurately. Since the tool is easily flipped over and the arms interchanged, be aware of the importance of placing the arm with the scale on it down first. It needs to be placed over the initial side of the angle, with the rivet over the vertex, before rotating the other arm counterclockwise to the terminal side. If students use a protractor, ask them to check their answer with the goniometer/angle ruler and vice versa. This gives them practice with both tools.

As students are working on the What If Situation B table and equation about Amelia Earhart’s journey, refer them back to their work with equations in 6th grade, Comparing Quantities or Variables and Patterns.

PLANNING FOR SUMMARY

As students are working on this Problem, look for how students are using the tools to measure angles accurately. Have students demonstrate how they find the angle measures.

SUMMARIZE

Teacher Moves: Language

SOLUTIONS AND STRATEGIES

Have students share the angle measures they found for the Initial Challenge and explain their strategies for using the tools. Have students share their angle measures and distance measures for the What If on Amelia Earhart’s journey.

Teacher Moves: Compare Thinking, I Used to Think... Now I Think...

MAKING THE MATHEMATICS EXPLICIT

Have students report their findings in a class discussion. Take time to explore all the strategies they used to arrive at their answers.

Have students record their measurements for some of the angles. Look for large discrepancies. If large discrepancies occur, have the group measure again. Discuss what might account for any differences in the measurements. In this discussion, students will begin to understand the issues involved in making precise measurements; relate this to the fateful journey of Amelia Earhart.

Suggested questions

  • How do you decide the number of degrees for angles between the 5° intervals on the angle ruler?
  • What things do you check to make sure you are making accurate measurements?
  • We didn’t always get the same measurements. Why did this happen?

Have students complete this sentence: “I used to think angles and angle measurement was…” and “Now, I think angles and angle measurement is…” to gain insight on their current understanding.

As you finish the mathematical discussions, have students reflect on the Now What Do You Know question(s).

problems.title: SAD 2.3 Vertical, Supplemental, and Complementary Angles

text:
Problem 2.3 Vertical, Supplementary, and Complementary Angles

The objective of this Problem is to develop student understanding and skill in working with the vertical, supplemental and complementary angles. In the Initial Challenge students will investigate the relationship among these angles. In the What If Situations they will write generalizations and use algebraic expressions about these relationships.

NWDYK

Describe what you know about angles formed by intersecting lines. Include parallel lines and the angles formed by a line that intersects the parallel lines in your description.

Arc of Learning

Generalizing and Using Properties of Polygons: Exploration/Analysis

Algebraic Expressions and Equations: Analysis

Key Terms

Parallel

Vertical angles

Supplementary angles

Complementary angles

Adjacent angles

Materials

Learning Aid 2.3A: Initial Challenge Cases

Learning Aid 2.3B: What If Situation A

Learning Aid 2.3C: What If Situations B and C

Teaching Aid 2.3A: Parallel and Non-Parallel Lines

Teaching Aid 2.3B: Complement Angles (optional)

Pacing

1 Day

Groups

Think-Pair-Share

A #13-19

C #26-27

E #32-34

Facilitating Discourse

LAUNCH

Teacher Moves: Language

CONNECTING TO PRIOR KNOWLEDGE

Use Teaching Aid 2.3: Parallel and Non-Parallel Lines to talk about parallel and nonparallel lines. Students were first introduced to parallel lines in elementary school. It will be helpful to briefly review the definitions.

PRESENTING THE CHALLENGE

Use the introduction in the student edition to introduce the setting of parallel lines in our lives. Launch the problem with the suggested question, “How do we determine or construct parallel lines?”

Note: Have a brief conversation with students after they've worked on the Initial Challenge

EXPLORE

Teacher Moves: Going Vertical

PROVIDING FOR INDIVIDUAL NEEDS

Having students stand up and work on a vertical surface during this problem can increase engagement and collaboration between students as they work out the relationships with these angles.

Suggested questions

  • Do any of the angles have the same measurement? How do you know?
  • Could any of the angles help you in finding the measurement of another angle?
  • Are there any “special” angles that could help you find relationships?
  • Does measuring the angles help you to see any new relationships
  • What relationships can help you find the measurements of the angles in What If A?
  • In What If Situation C, how did we write and solve equations in Variables and Patterns and Bits of Rational in 6th grade?

PLANNING FOR THE SUMMARY

Listen for how students are making sense of vertical, supplementary and complementary angles. Look for students who are using the relationships formed by a line that intersects the parallel lines versus actually measuring the angles to lead the discussions in the Summary.

SUMMARIZE

SOLUTIONS AND STRATEGIES

Have students share the relationships they found in the Initial Challenge before they work on the What If situations.

Suggested questions

  • What relationships among the vertical angles did you find in the Initial Challenge?

Have students share their evidence to prove or disprove their conjectures from their work on the What If situations.

Teacher Moves: Compare Thinking, Language

MAKING THE MATHEMATICS EXPLICIT

Suggested questions

  • What are some relationships you noticed in the angle measures in What If Situation A?
  • Do you agree with Jamal’s claim in What If Situation B? Why or why not?
  • How did you find the value of x for each figure in What If Situation C?

The variety of relationships among angles formed by parallel lines are very useful to know. Be sure students have those facts figured out (not necessarily by their familiar names of alternate interior, alternate exterior, and corresponding angles). A good way to deal with this in the Summarize might be to present a different sketch other than those offered in the Problem and ask students to start from the measure of just one angle to deduce all the other measures. Have them explain how they know the measure of an angle.

As you finish the mathematical discussions, have students reflect on the Now What Do You Know question(s).

investigations.title: SAD Designing Polygons: The Angle Connection

text:
Problem 3.1 Back to the Bees: Tiling a Plane

This Problem uses results about angle measurement in polygons to explain the tiling properties of polygons. The use of tessellations or tiling will help to solidify ideas that students are forming around characteristics of shapes and in particular angle measurements. In the Initial Challenge students will investigate tiling several polygons. In the What If Situations students look at the angle measures of polygons and tiling with more than one polygon.

NWDYK

Which regular polygons can be used to tile a surface? Explain why they tile. Give some examples of how tiling polygons can be useful.

Arc of Learning

Generalizing and Using Properties of Polygons: Analysis/Synthesis

Key Terms

Tilings

Tessellations

Materials

Large paper

Markers

Learning Aid 3.1A: Polygons to Test for Tiling

Learning Aid 3.1B: Initial Challenge Table

Shapes Set (or paper/digital shapes)

Teaching Aid 3.2: Honeycombs

Pacing

1 Day

Groups

Think-Pair-Share

A #8-10

C #26-20

E #40

Facilitating Discourse

LAUNCH

CONNECTING TO PRIOR KNOWLEDGE

Launch the Problem by asking students is they have seen honeycombs made by bees. Ask where they might have seen a similar pattern of hexagons, since it is a very common tile pattern.

Suggested questions

  • Why do these regular hexagons fit so neatly?
  • What other polygons do you think can be used to tile a surface?

Teacher Moves: Portrayal, Think-Pair-Share

PRESENTING THE CHALLENGE

Have students begin looking for shapes that will tile independently. Transition them to working with a partner after they’ve had time to experiment on their own. The goal is to find which polygons will tile and why. Have students record their findings on large sheets of paper that show drawings and explanations of their work and/or Learning Aid 3.1B: Initial Challenge Table.

EXPLORE

PROVIDING FOR INDIVIDUAL NEEDS

It will be helpful for many students to have the plastic shapes. This will give them a tactile and visual sense of what goes wrong with the non-tiling figures.

Suggested questions

  • Could you turn/flip the shape to see if it will fit together and tile?
  • What do you notice about the shapes that tile versus the shapes that don’t tile? Do regular polygons and irregular polygons tile?
  • What are some examples of polygons that tile?
  • What do you notice about where the tiles meet?
  • What does that tell us about the measures of the angles around the point?

Be sure students draw pictures to illustrate their answers.

PLANNING FOR THE SUMMARY

As you are circulating look for examples of tiling and non-tiling regular polygons for students to share in the Summary. Listen for the ways that students are generalizing the relationships they’ve found with the angle measures and tiling.

SUMMARIZE

SOLUTIONS AND STRATEGIES

Have groups share the shapes and combinations of shapes that they found would tile. Focus the discussion on why those work and others did not.

Teacher Moves: Claim, Support, Question

MAKING THE MATHEMATICS EXPLICIT

Students should be able to explain why there are only three regular polygons that tile, using angle measure as part of their argument. They should also be able to explain why certain combinations of regular polygons work, using angle measures.

Suggested questions

  • When you tried just a single shape, did all of your shapes tile?
  • With the shapes that did tile, what is the sum of the measures of the angles around each vertex point in a tiling?
  • What happens with the heptagon?
  • How did finding the shapes that tile help you with thinking about angle measurements?
  • Since we know that triangles, squares, and hexagons tile, what does this tell us about the measure of the angles if those are regular shapes?
  • What is the measure of one angle a regular triangle? A square? A regular hexagon?
  • What other combinations of shapes tile?

As you finish the mathematical discussions, have students reflect on the Now What Do You Know question(s).

At the end of this problem, you might want to share one of these videos.

  • What is a Tessellation? (Time 2:20) at https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=7GiKeeWSf4s
  • Why do bees love hexagons? (Time 3:58) at https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=QEzlsjAqADA

Problem 3.4 Designing Polygons

The objective of this Problem is to develop student understanding of the conditions that determine unique shapes. This is the foundation for future work on similarity and congruence. The storyline is a challenge to convey a lot of information with only a few words to produce a unique triangle.

NWDYK

What information about a triangle allows you to draw a triangle? Draw a unique triangle? Explain why this true? What information about a quadrilateral allows you to draw a quadrilateral? Explain why this true?

Arc of Learning

Generalizing and Using Properties of Polygons: Synthesis/Abstraction

Algebraic Expressions and Equations: Analysis
Key Terms

Materials

Learning Aid 3.4A: Message Cards

Learning Aid 3.4B: Possible Polygon Designs

polystrips, angle rulers, geoboards, dot paper, geometry technology, etc.

Pacing

1 Day

Groups

2

A #16-21

C #33-37

E #42-43

Facilitating Discourse

LAUNCH

CONNECTING TO PRIOR KNOWLEDGE

Earlier in the unit, students found that the sum of any two side lengths of a triangle is greater than the third side. They also found that given three side lengths that make a triangle, there is exactly one triangle. They learned that the sum of the angles of a triangle is 180°. In this Problem, they use this knowledge to look at the conditions that produce unique triangles and use their knowledge of angles to create other polygons.

Teacher Moves: Agency, Identity, Ownership

PRESENTING THE CHALLENGE

Launch the Problem by asking students, “Suppose you want to text a friend to give directions for drawing an exact copy of the figure. What is the shortest message to do the job?”

Have students brainstorm and share their ideas in their groups.

After some class discussion of approaches, you could segue to the Initial Challenge. Guide your students by suggesting that they look for some general guidelines they could use for writing their messages about triangles with minimum text and maximum information.

Note: There are 5 message cards on Learning Aid 3.4A. These could be divided up in the classroom with each partner group doing 2-3 message cards. Choose the message cards for each group based on the formative assessment you’ve been gathering on each student to meet their current needs.

EXPLORE

PROVIDING FOR INDIVIDUAL LEARNING NEEDS

As students work on the message cards, they should justify their answers. Encourage students to share their triangles on poster paper. You can use the posters in a Gallery Walk during the Summarize. At that time, students can add new information to their notes from the posters.

Students could use polystrips, angle rulers, geoboards, dot paper, geometry technology, etc. to determine if the triangles are possible.

As students are finishing the Initial Challenge give students cards from Learning Aid 3.4B: Possible Polygon Designs. Make sure each partner group gets at least one that is not possible.

Note: You can have them add this work to their posters for the Gallery Walk in the Summary.

PLANNING FOR THE SUMMARY

As you are circulating, take note of how students are justifying when triangles/quadrilaterals are and are not possible. Have students share these generalizations in the Summary. Look for students using angles and/or side lengths as their justifications.

SUMMARIZE

Teacher Moves: Gallery Walk

SOLUTIONS AND STRATEGIES

Start with a Gallery Walk of student created posters or have groups share their findings with the whole class. Ask the students where they notice differences. Students should be able to resolve these differences.

Teacher Moves: Claim, Support, Question, and Anchor Chart

MAKING THE MATHEMATICS EXPLICIT

Have students share thoughts, questions, and conclusions about the 5 message cards. Repeat a similar discussion with the What If 12 designs.

A conversation from one classroom:

Sandra: We thought there were three triangles for Message 1. (Shares the three they found, and they are the same triangle but oriented differently.)

Lewis: That is the same triangle but just turned on different sides. (Goes up to a poster and shows rotating the triangles to all be the same.)

Sandra: Oh. Now I see.

Arvin: We thought Message 4 was fun.

Teacher: What was fun in Message 4.

Arvin: Since we had all the angles for the triangle, we could create a lot of different triangles by just lengthening or shortening the sides once we had the angles set.

Shandra: We found that same thing with Design 2 in What If Situation A. We knew three angles and could find lots of triangles.

Teacher: What does this tell us about triangles?

Arvin:If we have three angle measures, we can make lots of triangles that have those angles.

Shandra: I agree. But, sometimes three angle measures do not form any triangles. We cannot just have any three angle measures. So, if you have three angle measures that make a triangle, then there are many triangles possible.

Teacher (writing on anchor chart): We have found that, “Many triangles are possible if we have three angle measures that make a triangle.”

As you finish the mathematical discussions, have students reflect on the Now What Do You Know question(s).
